facts.value: Two weeks after respiratory infection symptoms, dyspnea progressed to NYHA III with leg edema and abdominal pain; no chest pain or dizziness initially.
Ulcerative colitis controlled with mesalazine; past tobacco use.
TTE: preserved LV systolic function; dilated LA and RV; impaired RV function; severe tricuspid regurgitation; estimated systolic PA pressure 58 mm Hg; only mild mitral regurgitation.
CT pulmonary angiography: no pulmonary embolus; RV dilatation, bilateral pleural effusions and contrast reflux into hepatic veins.

args.summary: 35-year-old man with ulcerative colitis on mesalazine. About two weeks after a respiratory infection he developed NYHA III dyspnea, leg edema and abdominal pain. Heart rate is 42/min. ECG shows no P waves and a narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 42/min, which fits atrial standstill with a junctional escape. NT-proBNP is 432 and hs-troponin T is 31. TTE shows preserved LV function, dilated LA and RV, impaired RV function, severe TR and PASP 58 mm Hg. CTPA shows no PE, but does show RV dilatation, bilateral effusions and hepatic vein reflux (congestive hepatopathy). Cardiac MRI shows left atrial LGE with borderline T1/T2 edema and no ventricular scar. Together this suggests post-viral atrial myocarditis causing atrial standstill, with bradycardia and loss of atrial function leading to right heart congestion.
working_diagnoses: Acquired atrial standstill from isolated atrial (post-viral) myocarditis with junctional escape bradycardia and right-sided heart failure
Cardiac sarcoidosis or giant cell myocarditis affecting the atria
Hyperkalemia or drug-induced sinus arrest (to exclude)
next_actions: Check electrolytes (potassium), renal function, CRP and CBC with eosinophils
Continuous telemetry with transcutaneous pacing pads available; temporary transvenous pacing if the patient becomes unstable
Electrophysiology consult about permanent pacing; consider endomyocardial or atrial biopsy
Review whether mesalazine should be stopped

args.urgency: urgent – admit today to a cardiology telemetry/step-down bed
args.rationale: Heart rate is 42/min with a narrow-QRS escape rhythm and no P waves (ecg_005), consistent with acquired atrial standstill. This is causing right-sided heart failure: NYHA III dyspnea (hpi_001), peripheral edema (physical_exam_004), RV dysfunction with severe tricuspid regurgitation and PASP 58 (ecg_009), and pleural effusions with hepatic vein reflux (imaging_010). Cardiac MRI shows left atrial LGE with borderline edema (imaging_014), and troponin (lab_007) and NT-proBNP (lab_006) are raised. An urgent permanent ventricular pacemaker and IV furosemide 40 mg every 12 hours have been ordered. A narrow-QRS escape is usually fairly stable, but the escape rhythm could slow or fail. The patient therefore needs continuous monitoring with transcutaneous pacing pads on and a clear plan to escalate. Potassium, creatinine, TSH, CRP and eosinophils were not reported and must be checked right away.
args.followup_or_handoff: Handoff to inpatient cardiology and electrophysiology: (1) Continuous telemetry with transcutaneous pacing pads on. Keep atropine or isoproterenol at the bedside. Place a temporary transvenous wire if the escape rhythm slows, pauses or the patient becomes hypotensive or syncopal, and move to CCU/ICU if this happens. (2) Get stat electrolytes (especially potassium), creatinine, TSH, CRP, CBC with eosinophils, and repeat troponin. Correct any reversible cause before implant. (3) Check daily weights, strict intake/output, and kidney function and potassium while on diuresis. (4) EP study to confirm there is no atrial capture before VVI(R) pacemaker implant. (5) Myocarditis workup: consider biopsy and evaluation for sarcoidosis. Review whether mesalazine should continue, together with gastroenterology. (6) Consider genetic testing (SCN5A/NPPA) if the atrial standstill does not recover. (7) Repeat echocardiogram and cardiac MRI at follow-up, with outpatient cardiology and device clinic follow-up after discharge.
